structured_output.draft:
Ownership is a bundle of rights, and when a company can reach into your device and remove one of those rights after the sale, you don't own the device. You're renting it on terms you didn't negotiate, and the landlord can change the lease whenever they feel like it.

Think about what it means to buy a car. You hand over money, you get a title, and from that moment the car is yours — you can modify it, repair it, resell it, drive it into a lake if that's your thing. Now imagine the dealership retained a radio in the dashboard that let them disable your heated seats the moment you drove off the lot, and that the fine print you didn't read said that was always the deal. That's not a sale. That's a subscription dressed up as a purchase, and we should have the honesty to call it that.

John Deere has been doing something close to this for years (which is why right-to-repair has been such a live fight in farm country). Their tractors run software that reports back, that limits what independent mechanics can do, and that can render a $500,000 machine inoperable while your crops are rotting in the field. Deere calls this "protecting software integrity." What it actually protects is their monopoly on the aftermarket — their dealers, their parts, their labor rates. The machine is yours in the sense that you hold the loan. The functionality is theirs. I think the car analogy actually undersells how aggressive this is, because at least the dealer can't reach into your driveway.

Tesla does something structurally identical with features. You can buy a car with the hardware for a capability baked in, pay for access as a subscription, and then lose it the moment you stop paying — or, if you bought access outright and then resell the car, the next owner may find that what they bought isn't what they got. That's not an edge case or an oversight. It's a deliberate architectural choice to make the transaction reversible from one side only.

The legal scaffolding that makes all of this work is the End User License Agreement layered on top of the sale. The DMCA has been weaponized to make circumventing that software a crime, which means that even though you own the physical object, you can't touch the part of it that determines what it does. You've bought a house but the seller retained the mineral rights, and the courts are backing them up. That's a hell of an arrangement — for the company.

What we ought to demand is simple enough to state, harder to enforce: a device that's sold must be fully sold. If a feature exists in the hardware you purchased, the maker can't lock it remotely, can't make it contingent on an ongoing payment you didn't agree to at the point of sale, and cannot use software-license law to prevent you from fixing it yourself. We've managed to articulate this principle elsewhere. We have lemon laws. We have implied warranty of merchantability. We understand, in other contexts, that a sale is supposed to transfer something real.

The counterargument is always the same: innovation requires this model, companies need recurring revenue, the software is separate from the hardware. That's bullshit, and the separation is the tell. The software is what makes the hardware function, which means the software is the thing you're actually buying when you hand over the money. Carving it out is a legal fiction engineered to put all the risk on you — you absorb the depreciation, you're stranded with the hardware when the company kills the product line, you're barred from the repair market — while the company retains the actual value of the asset.

Ownership is not a courtesy they extend to you after the transaction. It is not a feature that can be patched away. It is the thing the transaction was supposed to be about, and we need laws that treat it that way.
